claim: Gross writes that in emergencies, where time is precious and the surgeons too few, the flap operation deserves a decided preference over the circular and over every other.

source.edition: S. D. Gross, A Manual of Military Surgery, second edition, Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1862 (entered 1861); clean OCR; the archive.org record dates it 1861

quote: In cases of emergency, where time is precious, and the number of surgeons inadequate, the flap operation deserves, in my opinion, a decided preference over the circular, and, in fact, over every other.

data.name_period: flap operation (preferred over the circular in an emergency)

scene.may_show: An amputation by the flap method in a hospital where time is short and surgeons are few.

claim: Gross writes that the main artery of the limb should always be thoroughly compressed by a tourniquet and not by the fingers of assistants.

source.edition: S. D. Gross, A Manual of Military Surgery, second edition, Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1862 (entered 1861); clean OCR; the archive.org record dates it 1861

quote: No blood should be lost during or after the operation, and hence the main artery of the limb should always be thoroughly compressed by a tourniquet, not by the fingers of assistants, who are seldom, if ever, trustworthy on such occasions.

data.name_period: tourniquet on the main artery during amputation, not the fingers of assistants

scene.may_show: A tourniquet compressing the main artery of the limb during the operation, not the fingers of an assistant.
scene.reduced_form: a tourniquet on a limb under a sheet

claim: Gross writes that when a limb has been struck by a cannon ball, fracturing the bones and tearing open the soft parts, amputation should as a general rule be performed.

source.edition: S. D. Gross, A Manual of Military Surgery, second edition, Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1862 (entered 1861); clean OCR; the archive.org record dates it 1861

quote: When a limb has been struck by a cannon ball or run over by a railroad car, fracturing the bones, and tearing open the soft parts, amputation should, as a general rule, be performed

data.name_period: amputation for a limb fractured and torn by a cannon ball

claim: The account of the Patriot Daughters of Lancaster says that, after the surgeon was sent for and the stretchers came, the amputation of the leg of a patient who had at first refused it was over in twenty minutes.

source.edition: Hospital scenes after the battle of Gettysburg, July 1863, by the Patriot Daughters of Lancaster (Lancaster: Daily Inquirer Steam Job Print, 1864; title page read)

quote: having tried in vain to persuade one of them, to have his leg amputated ... I sent for the surgeon, the stretchers came, and in twenty minutes it was over.

value.unit: minutes (from the stretchers' coming to the end of the operation, as the writer puts it)

notes: the patient was in a tent that the writer knew to contain rebels, at the tent hospital at Gettysburg (a Seminary hospital by the same text, see med.sites-west-north); one operation, one witness: a duration is never generalised
